'''John Gregory Taylor''' (born March 31, 1962) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] and [[kick returner]] with the [[San Francisco 49ers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He attended [[Pennsauken High School]] and was one of six NFL players to come from PHS during the 1980s. Taylor attended [[Delaware State University|Delaware State College]] and was a member of their football team, the Hornets. He was a member of the 49ers teams that won [[Super Bowl]]s [[Super Bowl XXIII|XXIII]], [[Super Bowl XXIV|XXIV]], and [[Super Bowl XXIX|XXIX]]. His younger brother is former safety [[Keith Taylor (safety)| Keith Taylor]].

'''Johnny Lee Stallworth''' (born July 15, 1952) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for 14 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]]. He played college football for the [[Alabama A&M Bulldogs football|Alabama A&M Bulldogs]], and was the Steelers' fourth-round draft pick in 1974. Stallworth played in six [[AFC Championship Game|AFC championships]], and went to four [[Super Bowl]]s, winning all four. His career statistics included 537 receptions for 8,723 yards and 63 [[touchdown]]s. Stallworth's reception total was a franchise record until being surpassed by [[Hines Ward]] in 2005. Stallworth played in three [[Pro Bowls]] and was the Steelers' two-time [[Most Valuable Player|MVP]]. He was inducted into the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2002.

'''John Milton Stephens''' (February 23, 1966 – September 1, 2009) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

Stephens played [[college football]] for the [[Northwestern State Demons football|Northwestern State Demons]] in [[Louisiana]], where he broke the program's career rushing record previously set by [[Joe Delaney]]. Following his senior season, he was selected by the [[New England Patriots]] in the first round (17th overall) of the [[1988 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1988 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1988/draft.htm |access-date=2023-09-24 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Stephens played in six NFL seasons from 1988 to 1993, the first five for the Patriots.  As a [[rookie]] for the Patriots during the [[1988 NFL season]], Stephens rushed for 1,168 yards and was selected to his only [[Pro Bowl]]. His final season, Stephens played in five games for the [[Green Bay Packers]] before being traded to the [[Atlanta Falcons]]  for cornerback [[Bruce Pickens]]. He was with Atlanta for only two weeks and played in no games for the Falcons before being released,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1993/10/26/Falcons-release-Stephens/1885751608000/|title=Falcons release Stephens |website=UPI.com |access-date=April 14, 2025}}</ref> and finished the season playing in seven games for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]].

Stephens was married to [[All-America]]n college swimmer [[Sybil Smith]]. Their daughter [[Sloane Stephens]], born in 1993, is a professional tennis player who won the [[2017 US Open (tennis)|2017 US Open]] women's singles title. His son [[John Stephens Jr.]] plays [[tight end]] in the NFL for the [[Dallas Cowboys]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/StepJo02.htm|title=John Stephens Jr.|website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] |access-date=January 28, 2024}}</ref>

Stephens was twice charged with rape. In 1994, after his final NFL season, he was accused of raping a woman at a Kansas City hotel.<ref>{{cite news |title=Former Patriot wanted for rape |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1994/09/04/Former-Patriot-wanted-for-rape/4242778651200/ |access-date=27 January 2022 |work=UPI |language=en}}</ref> He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to probation.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Crouse |first1=Karen |title=For a Rising Tennis Star, a Connection, Then Dealing With Loss |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/09/05/sports/tennis/05stephens.html |access-date=27 January 2022 |work=The New York Times |date=5 September 2009}}</ref> On September 1, 2009, Stephens died in a car accident while driving on a rural road near [[Shreveport, Louisiana]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nsudemons.com/news/2009/9/2/58462.aspx|title=Wreck claims NSU football great John Stephens|date=September 2, 2009|access-date=September 2, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131110130554/http://www.nsudemons.com/news/2009/9/2/58462.aspx|archive-date=November 10, 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref>

'''John Paul Skorupan''' (born May 17, 1951) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for eight seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1973 to 1980.

Skorupan was born in [[Beaver, Pennsylvania]], in 1951. He played [[college football]] for the [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Penn State Nittany Lions]] from 1969 to 1972. He was selected as a consensus first-team linebacker on the [[1972 College Football All-America Team|1972 All-America team]].<ref name=CAA>{{cite web|title=Football Award Winners|publisher=National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA)|year=2016|access-date=October 21, 2017|page=10|url=http://fs.ncaa.org/Docs/stats/football_records/2016/awards.pdf}}</ref>

He was then drafted by the [[Buffalo Bills]] in the sixth round (136th overall pick) of the 1973 NFL draft. '''John Robert Teltschik''' (born March 8, 1964) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[punter (gridiron football)|punter]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

Born in [[Floresville, Texas]], Teltschik played scholastically at [[Tivy High School]] in [[Kerrville, Texas]].<ref name="PFR1">{{Cite web |title=John Teltschik Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/TeltJo20.htm |access-date=June 1, 2024 |website=Pro Football Reference |language=en}}</ref>

He played [[college football|collegiately]] for the [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas Longhorns]], where he was the starting punter for the 1983-85 seasons.<ref name="NFL">{{cite web| url=https://www.nfl.com/players/john-teltschik/ |title=John Teltschik Stats |website=NFL.com |access-date=June 1, 2024}}</ref> As a sophomore, he was honored by [[United Press International]] as a second-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]], first team all-conference playing for a team that won the Southwest Conference Championship.<ref name="UPI 1983">{{cite news |title=Offensive Titans Nebraska, BYU Dominate UPI All-America |author=Dave Raffo |newspaper=Tyrone Daily Herald |date=December 8, 1983 |page=5 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/4574714/offensive_titans_nebraska_byu_dominate/ |via=Newspapers.com}}{{open access}}</ref> During his four years at Texas, the team went to (and lost) four straight bowl games. He set the school record for highest punting average in a game against Texas Tech in 1984 (surpassed by Michael Dickson in 2016) during which he kicked a 73 yard punt.<ref>{{cite web |title=Texas Longhorn Football Record Book |url=https://texaslonghorns.com/documents/2024/8/8/Football_Record_Book.pdf |access-date=16 September 2024}}</ref>

Teltschik was selected by the [[Chicago Bears]] in the ninth round of the [[1986 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1986 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1986/draft.htm |access-date=October 3, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He was cut by the Bears late in training camp, and was immediately picked up by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]].<ref name="KMS 1986.08.30">{{cite news |title=John Teltschik signs with Eagles |newspaper=Kerrville Mountain Sun |date=August 30, 1986 |page=five |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/kerrville-mountain-sun-john-teltschik-si/148484428/ |via=Newspapers.com}}{{open access}}</ref> He spent his entire four-year career with the Eagles,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=0mtIAAAAIBAJ&sjid=WFYDAAAAIBAJ&pg=4459,3190068&dq=john-teltschik&hl=en|title=The Victoria Advocate - Google News Archive Search|website=news.google.com|access-date=April 11, 2016}}</ref> leading the NFL in punts in 1986, 1987, and 1988 and punting yards in 1986.<ref name="PFA">{{Cite web |url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/playert/telt00200.html |title=John Teltschik Stats |website=Pro Football Archives |access-date=June 1, 2024 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200927194555/https://www.profootballarchives.com/playert/telt00200.html |archive-date=September 27, 2020}}</ref>

During his rookie year, he led the league in punts with 108 - the most ever for a rookie and 3rd most in NFL history. That year he was named the NFL All Rookie team and was the Eagles special teams MVP. He led the league in punts again the next year with 82, including a single-game NFL record 15 against the [[New York Giants]] (surpassed by [[Leo Araguz]] the next year); and was again named the Eagles special teams MVP. In 1998, he co-led the league with 98 punts. During his first three seasons he had 288 punts, handled some kickoffs, held for some placekicks, and made some tackles.<ref name="Where">{{cite web |title=Where are they now? P John Teltschik |url=https://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/where-are-they-now-john-teltschik |access-date=16 September 2024}}</ref>

In 1989, he injured his knee making a tackle. He played 7 more games before being pulled for the injury. He had 2 surgeries on his knee and it ended his career.<ref name="Where"/>

Teltschik returned to Texas and got into the home construction business before buying and operating a tree farm in Tioga, Texas.<ref name="Where"/>

'''John Skibinski''' (born April 27, 1955) is a former [[running back]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was drafted in the sixth round of the [[1978 NFL draft]] by the [[Chicago Bears]]. His NFL career was spent with the [[Chicago Bears]].<ref name="pro-football-reference">{{Cite web |title=John Skibinski Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/SkibJo21.htm |access-date=2024-05-23 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> and ran from 1978 to 1981. He spent the 1982 season out of professional football before returning to the game via the [[USFL]]; he played in the 1983 & 1984 seasons as a member of the [[Birmingham Stallions]] and [[Jacksonville Bulls]], respectively.<ref name="purduesports">{{cite web|url=http://www.purduesports.com/sports/m-footbl/archive/pur-m-footbl-ybyleads.html|title=PURDUESPORTS.COM - PURDUESPORTS.COM - Purdue University Official Athletic Site - Football|publisher=purduesports.com|accessdate=2016-07-28|archive-date=2016-04-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160421004434/http://www.purduesports.com/sports/m-footbl/archive/pur-m-footbl-ybyleads.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="justsportsstats">{{cite web|url=http://www.justsportsstats.com/footballstatsindex.php?player_id=skibijoh001|title=John Skibinski Statistics on StatsCrew.com|publisher=StatsCrew.com|accessdate=2016-07-28}}</ref>

He carried the ball sparingly during the 1975 season, as [[Mike Pruitt]] was the main threat for the Boilermakers but [[Hall of Fame]] coach [[Alex Agase]] saw his potential. In 1976, he was part of a power backfield with [[Scott Dierking]]. As the 1977 season approached, Agase had been replaced by [[Jim Young (American football coach)|Jim Young]], Dierking had graduated and moved on to the [[NFL]] and the highly touted Freshman [[Mark Herrmann]] was taking over at QB. Skibinski was voted team captain for the 1977 season and led the Boilermakers in rushing yardage (665 yards) and total offense (886 yards) and a record of 5-6 in [[Jim Young (American football coach)|Jim Young]]'s inaugural season at Purdue.<ref name="purduesports"/>  He was voted 2nd Team All-Conference following the 1977 season. He currently ranks #20 Career Rushing Attempts (339 carries); #18 Career Rushing Yards (1,605 yards) and #16 Career Rushing Average (4.7 yards/carry).<ref name="purduesports"/>

While at Purdue appeared in the 1977 [[East-West Shrine Game]], the 1978 [[Hula Bowl]] and the 1978 [[Japan Bowl]].<ref name="purduesports2">{{cite web|url=http://www.purduesports.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/122210aab.html|title=PURDUESPORTS.COM - Kyle Adams To Play In East-West Shrine Game - Purdue University Official Athletic Site|publisher=purduesports.com|accessdate=2016-07-28|archive-date=2016-09-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160915163416/http://www.purduesports.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/122210aab.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

He is the son of [[Joe Skibinski]], a former [[Cleveland Brown]] and [[Green Bay Packer]]. His father was also his high school coach at [[LaSalle-Peru High School|LaSalle-Peru]] Township High School in Illinois.<ref name="illinoisvalleyliving">{{cite web|url=http://www.illinoisvalleyliving.com/2012/09/20/gridiron-greats/ae8mxm0/?page=1|title=Gridiron greats | Illinois Valley Living|publisher=illinoisvalleyliving.com|accessdate=2016-07-28|archive-date=2016-09-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160919082221/http://www.illinoisvalleyliving.com/2012/09/20/gridiron-greats/ae8mxm0/?page=1|url-status=dead}}</ref>
